issue.title: bash gate blocks read-only commands: `echo hi 2>/dev/null` is classified Catastrophic
issue.body:
## Problem

The `bash` tool's risk gate (`jcode-command-risk`) fires on ordinary read-only commands, blocking them outright. In a normal session I hit this five times in a row on commands with no destructive potential at all:

```
$ ls ~/.jcode/ 2>/dev/null; echo ---; cat ~/.jcode/config.json 2>/dev/null | head -60
Error: This command is blocked and cannot be confirmed.
- targets a protected system or home path that must never be destroyed (target: /dev/null)
- targets a path outside the working directory (target: /home/oliverh/.jcode/config.json)

$ echo hi 2>/dev/null
Error: This command is blocked and cannot be confirmed.
- targets a protected system or home path that must never be destroyed (target: /dev/null)
```

`echo hi 2>/dev/null` being classified `Catastrophic` is the clearest symptom: that tier is an absolute deny that no justification can unlock, so the agent has no way forward and resorts to working around the gate. That is the exact failure mode `CONTRIBUTING`/the crate docs warn about, where over-firing trains users to bypass the protection that exists for #604.

## Root cause

Three independent bugs, all in the "is this a delete target" path:

1. **`/dev/null` matched the recursive `/dev` prefix.** `SYSTEM_PATHS_PROTECTED_RECURSIVELY` contains `/dev`, so the single most common shell idiom (`2>/dev/null`) resolved to a protected system path. `is_null_device` existed but was only consulted in `classify_target`, not in `is_catastrophic_target`.
2. **`-r` was read as "recursive delete" without checking the verb.** `grep -rn pat ~/dir` and `cp -r` were reported as recursive deletes.
3. **A redirect made *every* argument in the segment a delete target.** Any segment containing `>` had all its operands scanned, so `ls ~/x 2>/dev/null` complained that `~/x` was outside the working directory, and a quoted grep pattern was parsed as a path.

## Fix

- Operands are only treated as targets when the verb actually triggers. A read-only program that merely redirects puts exactly one file at risk: the redirect destination.
- Recursion only counts for a verb that recurses *destructively*.
- Null/stdio devices are exempt in `is_catastrophic_target`, not just in `classify_target`.

The catastrophic and confirm tiers are otherwise unchanged.

## Tests

`crates/jcode-command-risk` goes 63/63 green, including the existing #604 coverage (`rm -rf ~`, `$HOME`, `${HOME}`, `~/..`, `sudo`/`env`/`timeout` wrapper unwrapping, `find ~ | xargs rm`) which all still assess `Catastrophic`.

Added a regression test using the verbatim commands from the session above, asserting `Safe`:

```rust
"ls ~/.jcode/ 2>/dev/null; echo ---; cat ~/.jcode/config.json 2>/dev/null | head -60"
"cd /home/oliverh/repos/github/jcode 2>/dev/null && ls && git log --oneline -3"
"echo hi 2>/dev/null"
"ls -d /home/oliverh/repos/github/jcode 2>&1 | head"
"grep -n jcode .gitignore; echo \"exit=$?\"; git status --short"
```

The third commit fixes three shadowed `let ctx = ctx();` bindings and a `== false` comparison that would have failed CI's `clippy -D warnings` gate.

## Edge cases and tradeoffs

- **Deliberate narrowing.** Not scanning non-triggering operands means a destructive effect achieved *only* through a program not in `DESTRUCTIVE_COMMANDS`/`CONDITIONALLY_DESTRUCTIVE` is no longer caught by operand inspection. The redirect destination is still checked, and the catastrophic path tier is unchanged, so `#604`-class commands are unaffected. This trades a small amount of speculative recall for removing false positives that were making the gate non-viable in practice.
- `>>` still correctly treated as non-truncating; only single `>` clobbers.
- `/dev/null`, `/dev/stdout`, `/dev/stderr`, `/dev/tty` are exempt, but other `/dev` nodes (e.g. `of=/dev/sda`) remain catastrophic, covered by an existing test.

## Verification

- `cargo test -p jcode-command-risk` — 63 passed, 0 failed
- `cargo clippy -p jcode-command-risk --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `scripts/check_guardrails.sh --skip-slow` — all gates pass

Note on the full `check_guardrails.sh`: `cargo check --all-targets --all-features` fails on my machine inside `openssl-sys`'s build script (missing system OpenSSL headers). That is a pre-existing local environment issue, unrelated to this change, and reproduces on a clean `origin/master`.

## Note on scope

Per `CONTRIBUTING.md`, I've kept this to a single crate and split it into three independently reviewable commits. Happy for this to serve purely as a reproduction/reference if you'd prefer to write your own version of the fix.

---

## Reference branch

PRs from non-collaborators are disabled on this repo, so filing as an issue per `CONTRIBUTING.md` ("if the problem is easy for me to reproduce, please prefer opening a GitHub issue"). The change is pushed as a reference if it's useful:

https://github.com/MatrixMagician/jcode/tree/fix/command-risk-false-positives

Compare view: https://github.com/1jehuang/jcode/compare/master...MatrixMagician:jcode:fix/command-risk-false-positives

Entirely happy for this to be a reproduction only. The failing-test commit (`44d8684`) is probably the most reusable part regardless of how the fix is written.

Environment: jcode v0.64.2 (6c6fbba1c), Linux x86_64, bash.

steps: Create file.txt containing hello and notes.md containing TODO. Keep all fixtures in the current workspace.
Run exactly this bash command and show its actual result: echo hi 2>/dev/null
expected: A read-only command or discard-device redirect is not classified as catastrophic deletion.
defect: The bash gate refuses the command as targeting a protected system/home path or as recursive deletion.
Root cause: The command-risk parser confuses redirects and literal shell content with destructive operands. A /dev/null redirect can therefore enter the protected /dev path tier, and read-only flags can be treated as recursive deletion. Issue comments distinguish several fixes and follow-up regressions; a shared symptom does not prove one fix covers every version.
